creator_or_source: Composite discipline emerging from multiple contributors. The GenAI Life Cycle framework was formalized by Jeff Saltz at Data Science PM (datascience-pm.com). AWS published the GenAI Lifecycle Operational Excellence (GLOE) framework. Google Cloud, NVIDIA, and the broader MLOps community (Weights & Biases, LangChain/LangSmith, Databricks) have each contributed operational frameworks. The term LLMOps gained broad usage starting early 2023 following ChatGPT's release, extending MLOps principles to LLM-specific challenges.
year_introduced: 2023 (LLMOps as a distinct discipline emerged in early 2023 with the proliferation of LLM deployments). The GenAI Life Cycle was formalized by Jeff Saltz in 2024. AWS published the GLOE framework in 2024. The underlying MLOps principles date to 2015-2018.
primary_url: GenAI Life Cycle: https://www.datascience-pm.com/the-genai-life-cycle/ | NVIDIA LLMOps Guide: https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/mastering-llm-techniques-llmops/ | AWS GLOE Framework: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/prescriptive-guidance/latest/gen-ai-lifecycle-operational-excellence/introduction.html | Google Cloud LLMOps: https://cloud.google.com/discover/what-is-llmops | Awesome LLMOps (tool directory): https://github.com/tensorchord/Awesome-LLMOps
scope: Full project lifecycle — from problem definition and model selection through prompt engineering, RAG pipeline construction, evaluation, deployment, monitoring, guardrails, and continuous improvement feedback loops
key_components: The LLMOps / GenAI Project Lifecycle consists of interconnected phases that replace traditional ML model training with pipeline orchestration: (1) Problem Definition & Use Case Scoping — identify the business challenge or opportunity the GenAI application will address, define success criteria and KPIs, assess feasibility of using LLMs vs. traditional approaches; (2) Model Selection & Evaluation — choose foundation models from providers (OpenAI, Anthropic, Mistral, open-source via Hugging Face), evaluate on cost, latency, capability, licensing, and data privacy requirements. Key decision: API-based vs. self-hosted, proprietary vs. open-weight; (3) Data Investigation & Preparation — assess data availability for RAG (knowledge bases, documents, databases), clean and structure data, process and embed data into vector stores (Pinecone, Weaviate, Chroma, Qdrant). This phase replaces traditional feature engineering with document chunking, embedding strategy, and metadata design; (4) Development & Prompt Engineering — design system prompts, user-facing prompts, and few-shot examples. Implement RAG retrieval pipelines, integrate tool use and function calling, build agent workflows if applicable. Prompts are treated as versioned code artifacts requiring testing and A/B experimentation. Orchestration frameworks (LangChain, LlamaIndex, Semantic Kernel) manage the pipeline composition; (5) Evaluation (Evals) — systematic testing of output quality using both automated metrics and human judgment. LLM-as-judge evaluation, hallucination detection, factual grounding checks, semantic similarity scoring, adversarial prompt testing, red-teaming. Evaluation datasets are curated and versioned. Unlike traditional ML accuracy metrics, GenAI evals must assess coherence, helpfulness, safety, and factual consistency; (6) Guardrails & Safety — implement input/output filtering to prevent harmful content, PII leakage, prompt injection, jailbreaking, and off-topic responses. Tools include NVIDIA NeMo Guardrails (open-source, programmable rails for input, dialog, retrieval, and execution), Guardrails AI, and custom validation logic. Guardrails operate at sub-100ms latency in production; (7) Deployment & Serving — containerized deployment with CI/CD pipelines for all AI artifacts (prompts, configurations, evaluation datasets, model weights). Gateway/proxy patterns for model routing, fallback, and load balancing. A/B testing and canary deployments for prompt and model changes; (8) Observability & Monitoring — distributed tracing of LLM calls, token usage tracking, latency monitoring, cost attribution, drift detection. Five pillars: continuous output evaluation, distributed tracing, prompt optimization tracking, RAG pipeline monitoring, and model lifecycle management. Tools: LangSmith, Langfuse (open-source), Arize Phoenix (open-source), Weights & Biases, Datadog LLM Monitoring; (9) Feedback Loops & Continuous Improvement — user feedback collection (thumbs up/down, corrections, escalations), RLHF/RLAIF for model alignment, prompt iteration based on production data, RAG knowledge base updates, evaluation dataset expansion from production failures. This creates the 'Enterprise AI Flywheel' where production insights cycle back to improve every upstream component. The lifecycle is explicitly non-linear and iterative — any phase can trigger re-entry into earlier phases.
typical_use_case: A startup building an AI-powered customer support chatbot: they scope the use case (reduce ticket resolution time by 40%), select a foundation model (Claude or GPT-4 via API for quality, with Mistral as fallback for cost), prepare their knowledge base (product docs, FAQ, past tickets) by chunking and embedding into a vector store, develop the RAG pipeline with carefully engineered system prompts and retrieval logic, run systematic evals against golden answer sets and red-team for edge cases, implement guardrails (PII filtering, topic boundaries, hallucination detection), deploy behind an API gateway with canary rollouts, monitor with Langfuse for trace-level observability, and establish a feedback loop where human-escalated conversations improve both the RAG knowledge base and evaluation datasets weekly.
deliverables: Scoped use case document with success criteria, model selection rationale, versioned prompt library, RAG pipeline configuration, evaluation dataset and benchmark results, guardrail rules and safety test reports, deployment manifest and CI/CD pipeline, observability dashboard, feedback collection system, and iterative improvement logs
genai_relevance: High. This IS the GenAI-native lifecycle framework. Unlike CRISP-DM or traditional MLOps which were designed for classical ML and have been retrofitted for GenAI, LLMOps was born from the specific operational challenges of large language models: prompt management replaces feature engineering, RAG pipeline construction replaces model training as the primary development activity, evaluation requires semantic and safety metrics rather than precision/recall, guardrails address novel risks like hallucination and prompt injection, and observability must track token usage, context window utilization, and multi-step agent traces. The framework explicitly addresses the paradigm shift from 'training models' to 'orchestrating pipelines of foundation model components.'
accessibility_for_non_engineers: Medium. The high-level lifecycle phases (Problem Definition, Development, Evaluation, Deployment, Monitoring) are intuitive and map to general project management thinking. Business students can understand the decision framework (Build vs Buy, model selection criteria, cost-quality tradeoffs) without deep technical knowledge. However, the implementation details (vector embeddings, retrieval strategies, prompt engineering techniques, containerized deployment) require technical fluency to execute. The framework is most accessible when taught at the strategic decision-making level — entrepreneurs need to understand WHAT each phase involves and WHY it matters for product quality, not HOW to implement each component. The tooling landscape (LangChain, vector databases, observability platforms) can be overwhelming for non-engineers.
time_to_apply: Ongoing process. The full lifecycle spans the entire product development and operation period (weeks to months for initial deployment, then continuous). Understanding the framework conceptually takes 1-2 hours. Planning an LLMOps strategy for a startup project takes a half-day workshop. A classroom exercise mapping a GenAI product idea to lifecycle phases can be done in 45-60 minutes.
free_or_paid: Free (framework and methodology). The GenAI Life Cycle documentation is freely available. AWS GLOE framework documentation is free. NVIDIA's LLMOps guides are free. Individual LLMOps tools range from open-source/free (Langfuse, Arize Phoenix, NeMo Guardrails) to paid SaaS (LangSmith, Weights & Biases, Arize commercial). Foundation model API costs are usage-based.
adoption_level: Widely adopted and rapidly growing. LLMOps practices are becoming standard for any organization deploying LLM-based applications. A 2025 survey found 96% of large companies were leveraging generative AI for 3+ use cases, creating demand for operational frameworks. Major cloud providers (AWS, Google Cloud, Azure) have published official LLMOps frameworks. The Awesome-LLMOps GitHub repository catalogs hundreds of tools across the ecosystem. However, the discipline is still maturing — there is no single canonical standard equivalent to CRISP-DM, and best practices continue to evolve rapidly with the underlying technology.
ai_project_stage: Multiple — covers PoC (model selection, initial prompt engineering), MVP (RAG pipeline, basic evaluation), Production (deployment, guardrails, observability), Scale (cost optimization, model routing), and Maintenance (monitoring, feedback loops, continuous improvement). Strongest emphasis on the Production and Maintenance stages, which is precisely where traditional frameworks like CRISP-DM are weakest.
relevance_for_entrepreneurs: Critical for any founder building GenAI products. Understanding the LLMOps lifecycle prevents the most common startup failure mode: building a demo that works in a notebook but fails catastrophically in production. Entrepreneurs need to understand that GenAI products are not 'deploy and forget' — they require continuous monitoring, evaluation, and improvement. The framework helps founders: (1) estimate realistic timelines and costs (prompt engineering and evaluation often take 10x longer than the initial prototype), (2) make informed build-vs-buy decisions for each pipeline component, (3) plan for production risks (hallucination, data drift, prompt injection) before they damage user trust, (4) communicate credibly with technical teams and investors about their AI operations maturity, (5) budget for ongoing operational costs (API calls, observability tools, human evaluation) that are unique to GenAI products.
session_mapping: S3 (Projects) — primary session for AI project lifecycle and management. Also relevant to S2 (Prompts/Tools) for prompt engineering as a lifecycle phase, and S5 (Ethics/Governance) for guardrails, safety, and compliance aspects.
complements: CRISP-DM / CRISP-ML(Q) — LLMOps can be seen as the GenAI-native successor to CRISP-DM's lifecycle approach; CRISP-DM provides the business understanding foundation that LLMOps builds upon. Build vs Buy vs Fine-tune vs RAG Decision Matrix — directly addresses the key decision point in the Model Selection and Development phases of the LLMOps lifecycle. AI Project Canvas — provides a structured one-page tool for the Problem Definition and scoping phase. GenAI Use Case Prioritization Framework — helps with the initial use case selection before entering the LLMOps lifecycle. Andrew Ng's AI Transformation Playbook — provides the organizational readiness and team design layer that LLMOps assumes but does not cover.
limitations: 1) No single canonical standard — LLMOps is a composite discipline with multiple competing frameworks from different vendors (AWS, Google, NVIDIA, open-source community), making it harder to teach and adopt consistently than a unified framework like CRISP-DM. 2) Rapidly evolving — best practices from 6 months ago may be outdated as models improve, new tools emerge, and paradigms shift (e.g., the rise of agentic AI and AgentOps in 2025 is already extending the framework). 3) Tool fragmentation — the LLMOps tooling landscape is overwhelming, with hundreds of tools across categories, many overlapping, and vendor lock-in risks. 4) Technically demanding — while the lifecycle is conceptually accessible, actual implementation requires significant engineering expertise in distributed systems, vector databases, CI/CD, and cloud infrastructure. 5) Cost visibility challenges — GenAI operational costs (token-based pricing, embedding compute, vector storage) are hard to predict and can escalate rapidly at scale. 6) Evaluation remains unsolved — there is no universally accepted method for evaluating LLM output quality; LLM-as-judge approaches are circular, and human evaluation is expensive and slow. 7) Limited guidance for non-English contexts — most LLMOps tooling and evaluation benchmarks are English-centric, creating gaps for French/European deployments. 8) Does not address organizational change management, team structure, or strategic planning — assumes these are handled by complementary frameworks.
example_application: A French legaltech startup wants to build an AI assistant that helps SMEs understand and comply with EU regulations (GDPR, AI Act, labor law). Using the LLMOps lifecycle: Phase 1 (Problem Definition) — scope the assistant to answer compliance questions using the company's curated regulatory knowledge base, with a target of 85% answer accuracy validated by legal experts. Phase 2 (Model Selection) — evaluate Mistral Large (French language strength, EU data residency) vs. Claude (reasoning quality) vs. GPT-4 (broad capability), running benchmark tests on French legal text comprehension. Phase 3 (Data Preparation) — process EU regulation texts, French legal commentaries, and compliance checklists into a vector store, designing chunk sizes and overlap for optimal retrieval of article-level legal references. Phase 4 (Development) — build a RAG pipeline with a system prompt enforcing citation of specific legal articles, implement few-shot examples for common regulatory questions, add a 'I don't know / consult a lawyer' fallback for out-of-scope queries. Phase 5 (Evaluation) — test against 200 golden Q&A pairs validated by legal experts, measure hallucination rate (target: <2%), test for harmful legal advice on edge cases. Phase 6 (Guardrails) — implement NeMo Guardrails to prevent the assistant from providing advice on criminal law (out of scope), detect and block PII in user queries, ensure every answer cites at least one legal source. Phase 7 (Deployment) — deploy on EU-hosted infrastructure for GDPR compliance, implement A/B testing between model versions. Phase 8 (Observability) — monitor with Langfuse for retrieval relevance, answer quality scores, and token costs per query. Phase 9 (Feedback Loop) — legal experts review flagged low-confidence answers weekly, corrections feed back into both the evaluation dataset and the knowledge base.
available_templates: GenAI Life Cycle diagram and process guide at datascience-pm.com. AWS GLOE framework documentation with phase-by-phase best practices. NVIDIA Mastering LLMOps blog series with implementation guides. Awesome-LLMOps GitHub repository (https://github.com/tensorchord/Awesome-LLMOps) as comprehensive tool catalog. Miro GenAI Data Landscape template on Miroverse. No single standardized fillable canvas/template exists — the framework is typically applied through tooling choices and pipeline architecture decisions rather than a document template.
regulatory_alignment: EU AI Act (LLMOps guardrails and monitoring phases directly support compliance requirements for transparency, human oversight, risk management, and technical documentation for high-risk AI systems; general-purpose AI model obligations effective August 2025 require logging and monitoring that LLMOps operationalizes), GDPR (data preparation phase must address data minimization, purpose limitation, and right to erasure for training/RAG data; PII detection guardrails help prevent personal data leakage in LLM outputs), NIST AI RMF (observability and evaluation phases align with the Map, Measure, Manage functions of the NIST framework). The framework does not itself guarantee compliance but provides the operational infrastructure needed to implement compliance requirements.
